questions.question_text: A digital security keypad requires a $5$-digit passcode. Digits $0$ to $9$ may be repeated and order matters. How many different passcodes are possible?

options.why: Calculated $10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6$, assuming digits could not be repeated.
Multiplied $10 \times 5$ instead of evaluating $10^5$.
Used only $4$ digits instead of the required $5$ digits.

questions.solution_text:
Each of the $5$ positions has $10$ options ($0$ to $9$).
$10^5$
$= 100\,000$

questions.question_text: A company assigns employee badges with a code of $3$ letters followed by $4$ digits. Letters and digits may be repeated and order matters. Which expression gives the total number of possible badge codes?

options.why: Multiplied the pool size by the length rather than using powers.
Multiplied $26 \times 10$ and raised the product to the total length $7$.
Swapped the base and exponent for both letters and digits.

questions.solution_text:
There are $3$ letter positions with $26$ options each and $4$ digit positions with $10$ options each.
$26^3 \times 10^4$

questions.question_text: A school locker has a $3$-digit combination using digits $0$ to $9$, with repeats allowed. If the first digit is set to $7$, how many different combinations are possible?

options.why: Counted all $3$ positions as having $10$ choices, ignoring the fixed first digit.
Calculated $1 \times 9 \times 8$, assuming no repetition for the remaining two digits.
Multiplied $10 \times 2$ instead of evaluating $10^2$.

questions.solution_text:
The first digit is fixed as $7$ ($1$ choice), and the other two positions each have $10$ choices.
$1 \times 10^2$
$= 100$

questions.question_text: A secret password is made of $6$ letters, chosen exclusively from the $5$ vowels (A, E, I, O, U). Letters may be repeated and order matters. How many such passwords can be formed?

options.why: Multiplied $5 \times 6$ instead of evaluating $5^6$.
Calculated $5! = 120$, assuming $5$ positions without repetition.
Calculated $6^5$, swapping the base and exponent.

questions.solution_text:
Each of the $6$ positions can be filled by any of the $5$ vowels.
$5^6$
$= 15\,625$

questions.question_text: A smart-home network needs to assign a unique binary string (consisting of $0$s and $1$s) to each of $2000$ sensors. What is the minimum length of binary string required?

options.why: Calculated $2^{10} = 1024$, which is insufficient to cover $2000$ sensors.
Chose an unnecessarily large power ($2^{12} = 4096$) when $11$ is sufficient.
Calculated $2^9 = 512$, which covers far fewer than $2000$ sensors.

questions.solution_text:
Let $n$ be the string length. We require $2^n \geq 2000$.
$2^{10} = 1024 < 2000$
$2^{11} = 2048 \geq 2000$
The minimum length is $11$.

questions.question_text: A $3$-digit code is chosen from the digits $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$. How many more codes can be formed when repetition is allowed compared to when all digits must be distinct?

options.why: Gave the total count with repetition ($6^3$) instead of the difference between the two counts.
Gave the count without repetition ($6 \times 5 \times 4$) instead of the difference.
Calculated $6 \times 3 = 18$ instead of evaluating $6^3 - 120$.

questions.question_text: Four fair coins (a $10\text{c}$, $20\text{c}$, $50\text{c}$, and \$1 coin) are tossed simultaneously. How many different outcomes of heads and tails are possible?

options.why: Multiplied $2 \times 4$ instead of evaluating $2^4$.
Counted only the number of coins rather than the combinations of outcomes.
Calculated $4! = 24$, treating coin tossing as an arrangement without repetition.

questions.solution_text:
Each of the $4$ coins has $2$ possible outcomes (heads or tails).
$2^4$
$= 16$

questions.question_text: A genetics lab synthesises custom DNA tags using sequences of the $4$ bases (A, C, G, T). Bases may be repeated and order matters. What is the minimum length of sequence needed to produce at least $50\,000$ distinct tags?

options.why: Evaluated $4^7 = 16\,384$, which falls short of the $50\,000$ requirement.
Selected a length giving $4^9 = 262\,144$, which is larger than the minimum necessary length.
Evaluated $4^6 = 4096$, which is far below $50\,000$.

questions.solution_text:
Let $k$ be the sequence length. We require $4^k \geq 50\,000$.
$4^7 = 16\,384 < 50\,000$
$4^8 = 65\,536 \geq 50\,000$
The minimum sequence length is $8$.

questions.question_text: Using the digits $1$ to $9$ with repetition allowed, how many $4$-digit numbers can be formed such that the digits alternate odd-even-odd-even (O-E-O-E)?

options.why: Calculated $9 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6$, ignoring the alternating parity restriction and assuming no repetition.
Evaluated $3^4 = 81$, using $3$ choices per position.
Calculated $4^4 = 256$, using $4$ choices for every position.

questions.solution_text:
From $1$ to $9$, there are $5$ odd digits ($1, 3, 5, 7, 9$) and $4$ even digits ($2, 4, 6, 8$).
For the pattern O-E-O-E:
$5 \times 4 \times 5 \times 4$
$= 5^2 \times 4^2$
$= 25 \times 16$
$= 400$
